questions.q: Why can't you simply measure a qubit to 'check' it for errors the way you'd read a classical bit?
options: Measurement only works on qubits that are already in a classical 0 or 1 state
Reading a qubit always returns the wrong value
Measuring a qubit is physically impossible with current technology
Measuring a qubit in the computational basis collapses its superposition, destroying the amplitude information you were trying to protect
questions.explain: A classical bit read doesn't change the bit, but a qubit measurement collapses superposition and returns only one classical outcome, discarding the rest of the state information.

questions.q: Why are quantum errors described as more varied than classical bit flips?
options: Quantum errors can only occur during measurement, never otherwise
Quantum errors are identical to classical bit flips, just renamed
Quantum errors only ever happen to the |1> state, never |0>
A qubit's superposition can be corrupted by a continuum of small arbitrary rotations, not just a single discrete flip
questions.explain: Unlike a classical bit's single way of being wrong (flipped), a qubit's state can be perturbed by an arbitrary small rotation, in principle a continuum of possible corruptions.

questions.q: What physical fact rules out protecting a qubit with literal copies the way the classical repetition code copies a bit?
options: Copying qubits is allowed, but only if done before any gates are applied
The no-cloning theorem: no physical process can copy an arbitrary unknown quantum state
Qubits cannot be entangled with each other
Classical bits cannot be copied either, so this isn't actually a quantum-specific problem
questions.explain: No-cloning (covered in depth in the next lesson) is a direct consequence of the linearity of quantum mechanics, not a fixable engineering limitation -- it rules out copying an unknown qubit state outright.

questions.q: According to the lesson, how does quantum error correction achieve redundancy without literally copying the logical qubit?
options: By spreading the logical information across several physical qubits using entanglement, rather than making copies
By measuring the qubit directly and rewriting it if wrong
It doesn't achieve redundancy at all -- quantum error correction is impossible
By storing a classical backup of the qubit's amplitudes in a separate memory
questions.explain: Entangling the logical information across multiple physical qubits (the encoding step built concretely in chapter 3) is how quantum codes get redundancy without violating no-cloning.

questions.q: Why does the lesson claim that detecting only a small discrete set of error types (bit-flip and phase-flip combinations) is enough to handle the broader space of continuous quantum errors?
options: Measuring the error syndrome effectively forces a continuous error into one of a few discrete outcomes, without revealing the protected logical state
Continuous errors never actually occur in real quantum hardware
This is only true for classical repetition codes, not quantum codes
Discrete errors and continuous errors are mathematically identical with no distinction
questions.explain: Syndrome measurement projects the error (not the data) onto one of a discrete set of outcomes, which is exactly what makes a discrete-error-correcting code sufficient even though the space of possible small errors is continuous.
